claims.text: Local atomic lattice distortion caused by severe atomic-size mismatch is the primary mediator governing hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
The initial alloy is single-phase in the as-cast state.
The initial alloy has significant local lattice distortion.
Heat treatment can reduce lattice distortion while preserving the alloy's phase constitution.
Heat treatment can reduce lattice distortion without changing grain structure or grain size.
The proposed heat treatment does not form secondary phases or precipitates.
X-ray diffraction peak broadening can quantify the relevant local lattice distortion.
Pair distribution function analysis can quantify the relevant local lattice distortion.
Differences in constituent atomic sizes produce random fluctuations in local atomic spacing.
Random fluctuations in atomic spacing create local stress fields.
Local stress fields caused by lattice distortion obstruct dislocation movement.
Obstructing dislocation movement increases hardness.
Obstructing dislocation movement increases yield strength.
Reducing lattice distortion lowers the energetic barriers to dislocation motion.
A heat-treated sample with reduced lattice distortion should have lower hardness than the as-cast baseline.
A heat-treated sample with reduced lattice distortion should have lower yield strength than the as-cast baseline.
The proposed governing behavior is limited to single-phase high-entropy alloys for which grain size and precipitation are controlled.
Secondary-phase formation or grain coarsening may cause strengthening mechanisms other than lattice distortion to dominate.
Grain-boundary strengthening may contribute to hardness and strength under other processing conditions.

Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in both hardness and yield strength after verified distortion reduction would falsify the claim that lattice distortion is the primary governing mechanism.
